title: An eigenbasis simplifies repeated action
learningObjective: Decide whether an operator has an eigenbasis and explain the resulting diagonalization.

retrieve.bodyMarkdown: What happens to the matrix of a map when each chosen basis vector is only rescaled?

encounter.bodyMarkdown: A repeated stretch is easy to predict along eigenvectors. But a shear can have a repeated eigenvalue without supplying enough eigenvectors.

explain.bodyMarkdown: If the columns of an invertible $P$ are eigenvectors, then $AP=PD$ where $D$ lists their eigenvalues. Hence $A=PDP^{-1}$ and $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$ for positive integers $k$. An $n$-dimensional operator is diagonalizable exactly when it has $n$ independent eigenvectors. Distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors; a repeated eigenvalue may or may not supply enough. The identity is diagonalizable despite a single eigenvalue, while $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has only a one-dimensional eigenspace and is not diagonalizable.

reflect.bodyMarkdown: Multiplicity in the characteristic polynomial is not the number of independent eigenvectors. Count eigenspace dimensions, and state the field.

problems.promptMarkdown: A real two-by-two matrix has two distinct real eigenvalues. Which follows?

options.label: It is diagonalizable over the reals.
options.accessibleLabel: It is diagonalizable over the reals.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Count how many independent eigenvectors are available.
Distinct eigenvalues produce independent eigenvectors.
Two are enough for a basis in dimension two.
Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent. Two independent vectors in the plane form a basis, so diagonalization follows.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent. Two independent vectors in the plane form a basis, so diagonalization follows.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Solve the homogeneous system after subtracting the identity.
The off-diagonal entry is still one.
Only the first coordinate can vary freely.
The equation $(A-I)(x,y)=(y,0)=0$ forces $y=0$ and leaves $x$ free. The eigenspace dimension is one.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The equation $(A-I)(x,y)=(y,0)=0$ forces $y=0$ and leaves $x$ free. The eigenspace dimension is one.

problems.promptMarkdown: Which statement about a repeated eigenvalue is true?

options.label: It may or may not allow enough independent eigenvectors.
options.accessibleLabel: It may or may not allow enough independent eigenvectors.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Compare the identity and the shear.
Diagonalization requires a basis, not just roots.
The two examples have different eigenspace dimensions.
The identity has a full eigenbasis, while the shear in this lesson does not. Both have a repeated eigenvalue. Eigenspace dimension is decisive.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The identity has a full eigenbasis, while the shear in this lesson does not. Both have a repeated eigenvalue. Eigenspace dimension is decisive.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Follow the eigenvector through three applications.
Each application multiplies it by the same scalar.
The overall factor is the product of three twos.
Apply the relation repeatedly: $A^3v=2^3v=8v$. This avoids multiplying a full matrix three times.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Apply the relation repeatedly: $A^3v=2^3v=8v$. This avoids multiplying a full matrix three times.

problems.promptMarkdown: Prove that two eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues are independent.

steps.textMarkdown: Let $Au=\lambda u$, $Av=\mu v$, with $u,v\ne0$ and $\lambda\ne\mu$; suppose $au+bv=0$.
Subtract $\lambda$ times the original relation to obtain $b(\mu-\lambda)v=0$.
Since $v\ne0$ and $\mu-\lambda\ne0$, $b=0$; the original relation then gives $a=0$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Show a zero relation must have trivial coefficients.
Apply the operator to the relation.
Subtract a multiple of the original equation to eliminate one term.
Use the map to create a second relation and eliminate one vector. The distinct eigenvalues make the remaining scalar factor nonzero.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Use the map to create a second relation and eliminate one vector. The distinct eigenvalues make the remaining scalar factor nonzero.
